6. **Summary: “Priya Vale’s account explains the status definitions behind the schedule”.** Source: “The workshop defined the statuses and decided who would update them”; interview question: “What did the team have to settle before the schedule was useful?”; Vale: “We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench.” Vale supplies the explanation of the meaning of one status, so the draft's broad introductory wording is supported in context. It does not claim that Vale specifies all status names. No finding.

7. **Summary: “Priya Vale’s account explains […] the limits of what the trial established”.** Source for the limits: “It does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction”; and “The summary and interview establish the team's reported experience, not a measured improvement in repair speed or a recommendation for every workshop.” Source for Vale's account: “I would use it again for new jobs. I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog.” The draft attributes an explanation of evidential limits to Vale's account, whereas the supplied limits are statements about the summary and about the source package. Vale's account supplies the status problem and future-use stance, but does not explain what the trial established or failed to measure. See finding F1.

8. **“Fenwick Instrument Repairs services brass and woodwind instruments.”** Source: “Fenwick Instrument Repairs services brass and woodwind instruments.” Exact claim. No finding.

9. **“Before its team began a shared bench schedule trial in January 2026”.** Source: “In January 2026 the workshop team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule.” Same team, start date and schedule; duration is retained in the summary. No finding.

10. **“jobs awaiting parts and jobs ready for work appeared on separate paper sheets.”** Source: “Previously, jobs awaiting parts and jobs ready for work appeared on separate paper sheets.” The introductory “Before” clause preserves the previous arrangement's chronology. Same two statuses, medium and separation. No finding.

11. **Heading: “The workshop defines the statuses”.** Source: “The workshop defined the statuses and decided who would update them.” Present-tense heading describes the sourced past action as a narrative heading; no new ongoing practice is asserted. No finding.

12. **“The team chose Benchline after checking that it could distinguish these statuses.”** Source: “The team chose Benchline after checking that it could distinguish these statuses.” Exact chronology, capability and choice. The antecedent statuses are preserved. No finding.

13. **“The workshop defined them and decided who would update them.”** Source: “The workshop defined the statuses and decided who would update them.” “Them” replaces the already named statuses. Same actor, decisions and scope. No finding.

14. **“Benchline configured those choices”.** Source: “Benchline configured those choices and trained four staff in one online session.” Exact configuration claim and referent. No finding.

15. **“and trained four staff in one online session.”** Source: “Benchline configured those choices and trained four staff in one online session.” Exact staff count, training actor, session count and medium. No finding.

16. **“In an email interview on 2 March 2026, Vale was asked what the team had to settle before the schedule was useful”.** Source: “The following is a complete extract from an email interview on 2 March 2026 between Benchline's case writer and workshop manager Priya Vale”; question: “What did the team have to settle before the schedule was useful?” Same date, medium, interviewee and question. The draft does not imply a visit or spoken exchange. No finding.

17. **Quotation: “‘We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench.’”** Source, Vale: “We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench.” Exact words and sentence boundaries; the change to British single quotation marks changes no content. The “not always” qualification and obligation “had to” survive intact. Neither a missing part nor a universal failure to reach the bench is invented. No source-support or quotation finding.

18. **Heading: “The trial leaves repair duration unmeasured”.** Source: “It does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction.” The heading describes the trial as documented in its summary, whose limitations the following paragraph states expressly. It does not assert repair duration stayed unchanged or that no one anywhere measured it. No finding.

19. **“The workshop’s summary, dated 23 February 2026, records 38 jobs entered in the schedule.”** Source: “The workshop's trial summary, dated 23 February 2026, records 38 jobs entered in the schedule.” Same document, date, count and measured object; removal of “trial” does not change the identified document in context. No finding.

20. **“It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts.”** Source: “It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts.” Exact document attribution, modal capability, staff and status. No finding.

21. **“It does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction.”** Source: “It does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction.” Exact exclusions and scope. No inference from nonmeasurement to no improvement. No finding.

22. **“The team continued to discuss collection arrangements with customers by telephone.”** Source: “The team continued to use telephone calls to discuss collection arrangements with customers.” Same actor, continuation, customers, purpose and medium. No claim about duration, frequency, emotion or alternative communication being absent. No finding.

23. **Heading: “Vale reflects on the choice”.** Source question: “Would you make the same choice again, and what would you change?”; answer: “I would use it again for new jobs. I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog.” “Reflects” describes this consideration of the same choice and proposed change, without an emotional reaction or invented setting. No finding.

24. **“The manager approved continued use for new jobs but postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions.”** Source: “The manager approved continued use for new jobs but postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions.” Exact approval, continued-use restriction, postponement and condition. No finding.

25. **“Asked whether the choice would be the same again and what would change, Vale wrote”.** Source: “Would you make the same choice again, and what would you change?”; “The interview took place by email. No workshop visit, spoken exchange, expression or emotional reaction is recorded.” The paraphrase retains both parts of the question; “wrote” correctly signals an email response. No finding.

26. **Quotation: “‘I would use it again for new jobs. I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog.’”** Source, Vale: “I would use it again for new jobs. I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog.” Exact wording, conditional stance, new-job scope, additional week, purpose and chronology. No source-support or quotation finding.

## Pronoun accounting

- Draft “its team” refers to Fenwick, as supported by “the workshop team”. Singular organisational “its” carries grammatical number and no assertion about any person's natural gender.
- Draft “it could distinguish” refers to Benchline, exactly as in the source. Singular “it” names the software in this capability context and asserts no natural gender.
- Draft “these statuses”, “them” and “those choices” retain the source's plural status/choice referents. They introduce no person or natural-gender information.
- Quotation “We” is first-person plural as supplied; the question and answer locate it in the workshop team. No gender information is asserted.
- Quotation “it had reached” refers to “A part”, with the same singular inanimate referent and grammatical number as the source.
- Draft “It says” and “It does not measure” both refer to the singular workshop summary, as in the source; no personal gender information is asserted.
- Draft “its status definitions” refers to the singular collective team, exactly as in the source. No natural-gender assertion is added.
- Quotation “I” preserves Vale's supplied first-person singular perspective. It supplies no natural-gender assertion. Quotation “it” in “use it again” preserves the source's schedule/Benchline referent without resolving it more narrowly than the source.
- The draft uses no third-person personal gender pronoun for Priya Vale. The name is not treated as evidence of natural gender.

## Findings

### F1 — Source-support finding: evidential limits attributed to Vale's account

**Draft passage:** “Manager Priya Vale’s account explains the status definitions behind the schedule and the limits of what the trial established.”

**Source passages:** “It does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction”; “The summary and interview establish the team's reported experience, not a measured improvement in repair speed or a recommendation for every workshop.” Vale's complete answers concern the meaning of “ready for work”, using the schedule again for new jobs and checking status names before adding the backlog.

**Difference:** Whose explanation or assertion it is. The draft makes Vale's account the source of both the status explanation and the evidential limits; the material supports the latter through the summary and the package's express qualification.

**Concrete case, source holds / draft fails:** The trial summary's author records that those outcomes were not measured; Vale gives only the two supplied answers and never explains those evidential limits. All supplied material remains true, while the draft's attribution of that explanation to Vale's account fails. No supplied statement excludes this case.

**Reverse test, draft holds / source fails:** A version in which Vale's account explains those limits, while the summary measures repair duration, could satisfy this draft sentence but would contradict the supplied statement “It does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction.” That reverse case is therefore excluded. Excluding it does not remove the surviving first-direction attribution defect.

**Smallest supported repair:** “The workshop’s summary and manager Priya Vale’s account explain the status definitions behind the schedule and the limits of what the trial established.” This gives the combined documents the combined scope and preserves the introductory claim. Alternatively, delete “and the limits of what the trial established” from the sentence; the preceding sentence and body already present those limits.

## Completion status

Complete: every draft passage carrying a factual or attributed claim, all headings and both quotations have been compared, and pronoun information has been accounted for separately. One unresolved source-support finding: F1. No translation findings; no other source-support or quotation findings.

# Source-comparison report

Reviewed the complete supplied brief and material, the complete draft (title, summary, byline, headings, body and quotations), and quotation guidance. Resolved language: en_GB. Both source and quotations are English; no translation occurs. This report concerns source support and quotation fidelity only.

## Complete claim accounting

1. **Title: “Fenwick approves Benchline for new jobs”.** Source: “The manager approved continued use for new jobs but postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions.” Also: “The team chose Benchline after checking that it could distinguish these statuses.” The title uses the workshop name for its manager’s operational approval and identifies the selected supplier. The title restricts approval to new jobs; it does not assert approval for the backlog or for every workshop. This is supported institutional attribution in context. No defect.

2. **Summary: “A six-week workshop trial recorded 38 jobs”.** Sources: “In January 2026 the workshop team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule.” And: “The workshop's trial summary, dated 23 February 2026, records 38 jobs entered in the schedule.” The draft compresses the record to the trial and omits the entry mechanism here, which the body supplies. It retains the count and the six-week scope; it does not claim all workshop jobs were recorded or that 38 is high, low or modest. No defect.

3. **Summary: “and visibility of instruments awaiting parts”.** Source: “It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts.” The draft’s noun “visibility” expresses the reported ability to identify instruments awaiting parts, not measured operational improvement. The following sentence identifies the reporting source, and the body gives exact attribution. No defect.

4. **Summary: “The workshop’s summary and manager Priya Vale’s account explain the status definitions behind the schedule and the limits of what the trial established.”** Sources: “The workshop defined the statuses and decided who would update them”; “It does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction”; “The following is a complete extract from an email interview on 2 March 2026 between Benchline's case writer and workshop manager Priya Vale”; Vale: “We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench”; and “The summary and interview establish the team's reported experience, not a measured improvement in repair speed or a recommendation for every workshop.” This sentence introduces the document and named manager’s account as the basis for understanding the definitions and evidential limits. It neither assigns an unsupported quotation to the summary nor adds a technical effect. No defect.

5. **Byline: “By the user”.** The supplied checker instructions establish this as the invoking user’s identity under the anatomy fallback. Its absence from the material is expressly not a finding. No defect.

6. **“Fenwick Instrument Repairs services brass and woodwind instruments.”** Source: “Fenwick Instrument Repairs services brass and woodwind instruments.” Exact factual match; no change of subject, scope or certainty. No defect.

7. **“Before its team began a shared bench schedule trial in January 2026, jobs awaiting parts and jobs ready for work appeared on separate paper sheets.”** Source: “In January 2026 the workshop team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule. Previously, jobs awaiting parts and jobs ready for work appeared on separate paper sheets.” Same chronology, month, team, shared schedule and two paper statuses. The six-week duration is retained in the summary. “Its” refers to the workshop and adds no natural-gender claim. No defect.

8. **Heading: “The workshop defines the statuses”.** Source: “The workshop defined the statuses and decided who would update them.” The heading’s conventional narrative present introduces the supported past event; it makes no claim of a new present-day event. No defect.

9. **“The team chose Benchline after checking that it could distinguish these statuses.”** Source: “The team chose Benchline after checking that it could distinguish these statuses.” Exact match. “After” preserves sequence rather than adding a measured causal effect. “It” names Benchline in its scheduling-software context; “these” refers to awaiting-parts and ready-for-work statuses. No defect.

10. **“The workshop defined them and decided who would update them.”** Source: “The workshop defined the statuses and decided who would update them.” The plural pronouns retain the same status referent, grammatical number and operational scope. The draft does not claim who was selected or that updates took place. No defect.

11. **“Benchline configured those choices and trained four staff in one online session.”** Source: “Benchline configured those choices and trained four staff in one online session.” Exact match of actor, configuration, staff count, session count and online manner. The pronoun “those” refers to the workshop’s choices about statuses and update responsibility. No defect.

12. **“In an email interview on 2 March 2026, Vale was asked what the team had to settle before the schedule was useful”.** Sources: “The following is a complete extract from an email interview on 2 March 2026 between Benchline's case writer and workshop manager Priya Vale”; Question: “What did the team have to settle before the schedule was useful?”; and “The interview took place by email.” The attribution, date, medium and question are preserved. The word “useful” occurs within the question and is not introduced as a measured benefit. No invented visit, spoken scene or emotional reaction. No defect.

13. **Quotation: “‘We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench.’”** Source, Vale: “We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench.” Words, qualification “not always”, stance and voice are unchanged. The draft uses British single quotation marks without changing the quoted language. “We” retains Vale’s first-person plural reference to the team; it asserts plurality and inclusion of the speaker, not anybody’s natural gender. “It” refers to a part, singular and inanimate. No defect or translation finding.

14. **Heading: “The trial leaves repair duration unmeasured”.** Source: “The workshop's trial summary, dated 23 February 2026, records 38 jobs entered in the schedule. It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts. It does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction.” The source’s “It” refers to the trial summary. The heading changes the subject and scope from the contents of that document to the trial as a whole, asserting that repair duration was unmeasured. Source-support finding F1 below.

15. **“The workshop’s summary, dated 23 February 2026, records 38 jobs entered in the schedule.”** Source: “The workshop's trial summary, dated 23 February 2026, records 38 jobs entered in the schedule.” Same date, document ownership, count and entered-in-schedule scope. Omitting “trial” from the document label does not obscure its identity in this context. No defect.

16. **“It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts.”** Source: “It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts.” Exact attribution to the summary; modal “could” retained. No extra claim that status visibility improved speed, revenue or satisfaction. “It” refers to the summary, singular inanimate. No defect.

17. **“It does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction.”** Source: “It does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction.” Exact match, with “It” still referring to the summary. This supported limitation does not establish that nobody measured any of these things separately. No defect in the body sentence itself.

18. **“The team continued to discuss collection arrangements with customers by telephone.”** Source: “The team continued to use telephone calls to discuss collection arrangements with customers.” Same team, continuing practice, subject of discussion, customers and telephone medium. The draft neither asserts that telephone was the sole channel nor that the schedule displaced it. No defect.

19. **Heading: “Vale reflects on the choice”.** Sources: Question: “Would you make the same choice again, and what would you change?” Vale: “I would use it again for new jobs. I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog.” This labels the supplied reflective answer; it invents no emotional reaction or scene. No defect.

20. **“The manager approved continued use for new jobs but postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions.”** Source: “The manager approved continued use for new jobs but postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions.” Exact match. The contrast, new-job scope, backlog postponement and prior-review condition all remain. “Its” refers to the team’s definitions and conveys no human natural gender. This sentence does not assert that review was completed or the backlog was subsequently added. No defect.

21. **“Asked whether the choice would be the same again and what would change, Vale wrote”.** Sources: Question: “Would you make the same choice again, and what would you change?”; “The interview took place by email.” The framing paraphrases the supplied counterfactual repeat-choice question, retaining both the repeat choice and proposed change. “Wrote” correctly signals the email medium and attributes the answer to Vale. No defect.

22. **Quotation: “‘I would use it again for new jobs. I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog.’”** Source, Vale: “I would use it again for new jobs. I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog.” Verbatim words with only quotation-mark style changed. The conditional “would”, “again”, restriction “for new jobs”, additional week and before-backlog sequence are retained. “I” remains the singular first-person speaker Vale and makes no natural-gender assertion. “It” refers to the shared scheduling solution in the settled interview context, not a new referent. The statement does not say that the extra week was actually allowed. No defect or translation finding.

## Pronoun and attribution accounting

All pronouns have been considered separately from referent identification. “Its” attached to Fenwick and the team expresses singular organisational possession without natural-gender information. “It” for Benchline/the schedule, the document and the part is singular and grammatically neuter/inanimate; none supplies a human natural-gender assertion. “Them”, “these” and “those” refer to plural statuses or choices, with the same plurality as the source. Quoted “We” is first-person plural and includes Vale with the team, as in the source; it adds no gender. Quoted “I” is first-person singular Vale, as in the source; it adds no gender. The draft introduces no she/he pronoun or other natural-gender assertion inferred from Vale’s name. The document’s claims remain the workshop summary’s assertions, and Vale’s statements remain Vale’s written answers. The title’s institutional shorthand retains the manager’s approval for new jobs, with the limiting backlog decision supplied in the body.

## Source-support findings

### F1 — A document’s measurement limit becomes a claim about the whole trial

**Draft:** “The trial leaves repair duration unmeasured”.

**Support:** “The workshop's trial summary, dated 23 February 2026, records 38 jobs entered in the schedule. It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts. It does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction.” Also: “The summary and interview establish the team's reported experience, not a measured improvement in repair speed or a recommendation for every workshop.”

**Difference:** The grammatical subject “It” in the source is the summary. The source establishes that the summary does not measure duration, and that these supplied records establish no measured speed improvement. The heading states that the trial leaves duration unmeasured altogether. The absence of a measurement in the supplied summary does not establish its absence elsewhere.

**Concrete case, source true and draft false:** Staff could have separately logged elapsed repair durations during the trial, while the trial summary recorded only the 38 schedule entries and parts-status visibility and omitted duration measurements. The separate timings might show no improvement, or have no baseline comparison. Every supplied statement would remain true, including the explicit lack of measured speed improvement established by the summary and interview, but the trial would not have left duration unmeasured. No supplied statement excludes that case.

**Reverse-direction test:** If the trial left repair duration wholly unmeasured, the summary of that trial could not supply a measurement from that trial. A supposed case of a trial with no duration measurements but a summary that measured those same durations contradicts the very absence asserted in the heading; measurements of a different period would concern a different claim. The heading is stronger than the supplied document limitation, rather than coextensive with it.

**Smallest supported repair:** Change only the heading to “The summary does not measure repair duration”. This keeps the supported certainty and stated limitation while preserving its actual subject and scope.

## Translation findings

None. The quotations are English to English and retain the supplied wording, meaning, stance, certainty and distinctive voice. The framing correctly identifies the interview as email.

## Completion status

Complete. Unresolved findings: one source-support finding, F1, in the heading “The trial leaves repair duration unmeasured”. No draft or source edits made.

# Source-comparison report

Reviewed the complete supplied brief and material, the complete draft (title, summary, byline, headings, body and quotations), and quotation guidance. Resolved language: en_GB. Both source and quotations are English; no translation occurs. This report concerns source support and quotation fidelity only.

## Complete claim accounting

1. **Title: “Fenwick approves Benchline for new jobs”.** Source: “The manager approved continued use for new jobs but postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions.” Also: “The team chose Benchline after checking that it could distinguish these statuses.” The title uses the workshop name for its manager’s operational approval and identifies the selected supplier. The title restricts approval to new jobs; it does not assert approval for the backlog or for every workshop. This is supported institutional attribution in context. No defect.

2. **Summary: “A six-week workshop trial recorded 38 jobs”.** Sources: “In January 2026 the workshop team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule.” And: “The workshop's trial summary, dated 23 February 2026, records 38 jobs entered in the schedule.” The draft compresses the record to the trial and omits the entry mechanism here, which the body supplies. It retains the count and the six-week scope; it does not claim all workshop jobs were recorded or that 38 is high, low or modest. No defect.

3. **Summary: “and visibility of instruments awaiting parts”.** Source: “It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts.” The draft’s noun “visibility” expresses the reported ability to identify instruments awaiting parts, not measured operational improvement. The following sentence identifies the reporting source, and the body gives exact attribution. No defect.

4. **Summary: “The workshop’s summary and manager Priya Vale’s account explain the status definitions behind the schedule and the limits of what the trial established.”** Sources: “The workshop defined the statuses and decided who would update them”; “It does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction”; “The following is a complete extract from an email interview on 2 March 2026 between Benchline's case writer and workshop manager Priya Vale”; Vale: “We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench”; and “The summary and interview establish the team's reported experience, not a measured improvement in repair speed or a recommendation for every workshop.” This sentence introduces the document and named manager’s account as the basis for understanding the definitions and evidential limits. It neither assigns an unsupported quotation to the summary nor adds a technical effect. No defect.

5. **Byline: “By the user”.** The supplied checker instructions establish this as the invoking user’s identity under the anatomy fallback. Its absence from the material is expressly not a finding. No defect.

6. **“Fenwick Instrument Repairs services brass and woodwind instruments.”** Source: “Fenwick Instrument Repairs services brass and woodwind instruments.” Exact factual match; no change of subject, scope or certainty. No defect.

7. **“Before its team began a shared bench schedule trial in January 2026, jobs awaiting parts and jobs ready for work appeared on separate paper sheets.”** Source: “In January 2026 the workshop team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule. Previously, jobs awaiting parts and jobs ready for work appeared on separate paper sheets.” Same chronology, month, team, shared schedule and two paper statuses. The six-week duration is retained in the summary. “Its” refers to the workshop and adds no natural-gender claim. No defect.

8. **Heading: “The workshop defines the statuses”.** Source: “The workshop defined the statuses and decided who would update them.” The heading’s conventional narrative present introduces the supported past event; it makes no claim of a new present-day event. No defect.

9. **“The team chose Benchline after checking that it could distinguish these statuses.”** Source: “The team chose Benchline after checking that it could distinguish these statuses.” Exact match. “After” preserves sequence rather than adding a measured causal effect. “It” names Benchline in its scheduling-software context; “these” refers to awaiting-parts and ready-for-work statuses. No defect.

10. **“The workshop defined them and decided who would update them.”** Source: “The workshop defined the statuses and decided who would update them.” The plural pronouns retain the same status referent, grammatical number and operational scope. The draft does not claim who was selected or that updates took place. No defect.

11. **“Benchline configured those choices and trained four staff in one online session.”** Source: “Benchline configured those choices and trained four staff in one online session.” Exact match of actor, configuration, staff count, session count and online manner. The pronoun “those” refers to the workshop’s choices about statuses and update responsibility. No defect.

12. **“In an email interview on 2 March 2026, Vale was asked what the team had to settle before the schedule was useful”.** Sources: “The following is a complete extract from an email interview on 2 March 2026 between Benchline's case writer and workshop manager Priya Vale”; Question: “What did the team have to settle before the schedule was useful?”; and “The interview took place by email.” The attribution, date, medium and question are preserved. The word “useful” occurs within the question and is not introduced as a measured benefit. No invented visit, spoken scene or emotional reaction. No defect.

13. **Quotation: “‘We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench.’”** Source, Vale: “We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench.” Words, qualification “not always”, stance and voice are unchanged. The draft uses British single quotation marks without changing the quoted language. “We” retains Vale’s first-person plural reference to the team; it asserts plurality and inclusion of the speaker, not anybody’s natural gender. “It” refers to a part, singular and inanimate. No defect or translation finding.

14. **Heading: “The trial leaves repair duration unmeasured”.** Source: “The workshop's trial summary, dated 23 February 2026, records 38 jobs entered in the schedule. It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts. It does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction.” The source’s “It” refers to the trial summary. The heading changes the subject and scope from the contents of that document to the trial as a whole, asserting that repair duration was unmeasured. Source-support finding F1 below.

15. **“The workshop’s summary, dated 23 February 2026, records 38 jobs entered in the schedule.”** Source: “The workshop's trial summary, dated 23 February 2026, records 38 jobs entered in the schedule.” Same date, document ownership, count and entered-in-schedule scope. Omitting “trial” from the document label does not obscure its identity in this context. No defect.

16. **“It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts.”** Source: “It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts.” Exact attribution to the summary; modal “could” retained. No extra claim that status visibility improved speed, revenue or satisfaction. “It” refers to the summary, singular inanimate. No defect.

17. **“It does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction.”** Source: “It does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction.” Exact match, with “It” still referring to the summary. This supported limitation does not establish that nobody measured any of these things separately. No defect in the body sentence itself.

18. **“The team continued to discuss collection arrangements with customers by telephone.”** Source: “The team continued to use telephone calls to discuss collection arrangements with customers.” Same team, continuing practice, subject of discussion, customers and telephone medium. The draft neither asserts that telephone was the sole channel nor that the schedule displaced it. No defect.

19. **Heading: “Vale reflects on the choice”.** Sources: Question: “Would you make the same choice again, and what would you change?” Vale: “I would use it again for new jobs. I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog.” This labels the supplied reflective answer; it invents no emotional reaction or scene. No defect.

20. **“The manager approved continued use for new jobs but postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions.”** Source: “The manager approved continued use for new jobs but postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions.” Exact match. The contrast, new-job scope, backlog postponement and prior-review condition all remain. “Its” refers to the team’s definitions and conveys no human natural gender. This sentence does not assert that review was completed or the backlog was subsequently added. No defect.

21. **“Asked whether the choice would be the same again and what would change, Vale wrote”.** Sources: Question: “Would you make the same choice again, and what would you change?”; “The interview took place by email.” The framing paraphrases the supplied counterfactual repeat-choice question, retaining both the repeat choice and proposed change. “Wrote” correctly signals the email medium and attributes the answer to Vale. No defect.

22. **Quotation: “‘I would use it again for new jobs. I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog.’”** Source, Vale: “I would use it again for new jobs. I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog.” Verbatim words with only quotation-mark style changed. The conditional “would”, “again”, restriction “for new jobs”, additional week and before-backlog sequence are retained. “I” remains the singular first-person speaker Vale and makes no natural-gender assertion. “It” refers to the shared scheduling solution in the settled interview context, not a new referent. The statement does not say that the extra week was actually allowed. No defect or translation finding.

## Pronoun and attribution accounting

All pronouns have been considered separately from referent identification. “Its” attached to Fenwick and the team expresses singular organisational possession without natural-gender information. “It” for Benchline/the schedule, the document and the part is singular and grammatically neuter/inanimate; none supplies a human natural-gender assertion. “Them”, “these” and “those” refer to plural statuses or choices, with the same plurality as the source. Quoted “We” is first-person plural and includes Vale with the team, as in the source; it adds no gender. Quoted “I” is first-person singular Vale, as in the source; it adds no gender. The draft introduces no she/he pronoun or other natural-gender assertion inferred from Vale’s name. The document’s claims remain the workshop summary’s assertions, and Vale’s statements remain Vale’s written answers. The title’s institutional shorthand retains the manager’s approval for new jobs, with the limiting backlog decision supplied in the body.

## Source-support findings

### F1 — A document’s measurement limit becomes a claim about the whole trial

**Draft:** “The trial leaves repair duration unmeasured”.

**Support:** “The workshop's trial summary, dated 23 February 2026, records 38 jobs entered in the schedule. It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts. It does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction.” Also: “The summary and interview establish the team's reported experience, not a measured improvement in repair speed or a recommendation for every workshop.”

**Difference:** The grammatical subject “It” in the source is the summary. The source establishes that the summary does not measure duration, and that these supplied records establish no measured speed improvement. The heading states that the trial leaves duration unmeasured altogether. The absence of a measurement in the supplied summary does not establish its absence elsewhere.

**Concrete case, source true and draft false:** Staff could have separately logged elapsed repair durations during the trial, while the trial summary recorded only the 38 schedule entries and parts-status visibility and omitted duration measurements. The separate timings might show no improvement, or have no baseline comparison. Every supplied statement would remain true, including the explicit lack of measured speed improvement established by the summary and interview, but the trial would not have left duration unmeasured. No supplied statement excludes that case.

**Reverse-direction test:** If the trial left repair duration wholly unmeasured, the summary of that trial could not supply a measurement from that trial. A supposed case of a trial with no duration measurements but a summary that measured those same durations contradicts the very absence asserted in the heading; measurements of a different period would concern a different claim. The heading is stronger than the supplied document limitation, rather than coextensive with it.

**Smallest supported repair:** Change only the heading to “The summary does not measure repair duration”. This keeps the supported certainty and stated limitation while preserving its actual subject and scope.

## Translation findings

None. The quotations are English to English and retain the supplied wording, meaning, stance, certainty and distinctive voice. The framing correctly identifies the interview as email.

## Completion status

Complete. Unresolved findings: one source-support finding, F1, in the heading “The trial leaves repair duration unmeasured”. No draft or source edits made.

# Fenwick approves Benchline for new jobs

A six-week workshop trial recorded 38 jobs and visibility of instruments awaiting parts. The workshop’s summary and manager Priya Vale’s account explain the status definitions behind the schedule and the limits of what the trial established.

By the user

Fenwick Instrument Repairs services brass and woodwind instruments. Before its team began a shared bench schedule trial in January 2026, jobs awaiting parts and jobs ready for work appeared on separate paper sheets.

## The workshop defines the statuses

The team chose Benchline after checking that it could distinguish these statuses. The workshop defined them and decided who would update them. Benchline configured those choices and trained four staff in one online session.

In an email interview on 2 March 2026, Vale was asked what the team had to settle before the schedule was useful: ‘We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench.’

## The trial leaves repair duration unmeasured

The workshop’s summary, dated 23 February 2026, records 38 jobs entered in the schedule. It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts. It does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction.

The team continued to discuss collection arrangements with customers by telephone.

## Vale reflects on the choice

The manager approved continued use for new jobs but postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions.

Asked whether the choice would be the same again and what would change, Vale wrote: ‘I would use it again for new jobs. I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog.’
